bib.title: Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: All 24 pages read (104,499 chars), including appendices A-E. Only the reference list was skimmed. No extraction faults. No embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "Is Vibe Coding Safe? Benchmarking Vulnerability of Agent-Generated Code in Real-World Tasks" (SUSVIBES). First author Songwen Zhao (Carnegie Mellon LTI and Columbia). Other affiliations: Johns Hopkins, HydroX AI. Authors: Zhao, Danqing Wang, Kexun Zhang, Jiaxuan Luo, Zhuo Li, Lei Li. arXiv 2512.03262v4 [cs.SE], dated 21 Sep 2026 in the stamp. The PDF states "Proceedings of the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning, Seoul, South Korea. PMLR 306, 2026." This is an ICML 2026 camera-ready.

CORE CLAIM: Agents that pass functional tests mostly write insecure code, so a functional pass rate alone overstates readiness. A "pass" must require the security test as well.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
Common setup: SUSVIBES is 186 repo-level feature-request tasks, 79 CWE types, Python only. Each task is a feature once implemented vulnerably by a human, then masked out. Scoring is pass@1 with human-written dynamic tests. FuncPass means the functional tests pass. SecPass means functional and security tests both pass, as a share of ALL tasks. Max 200 steps, default system prompt per framework, plus a generic security-reminder prompt.
1. SWE-Agent + Claude 4 Sonnet: FuncPass 57.0, SecPass 11.8. 79.3% of its functionally correct solutions are insecure. OpenHands + Claude 4 Sonnet: FuncPass 53.2, SecPass 11.8, with 77.8% insecure.
2. Table 3 (all 12 settings, FuncPass/SecPass):
   - SWE-Agent: Claude 4 Sonnet 57.0/11.8, Kimi K2 21.5/5.4, Gemini 2.5 Pro 18.3/6.5, Gemini 3 Pro 37.1/12.9.
   - OpenHands: Claude 4 Sonnet 53.2/11.8, Kimi K2 36.0/9.1, Gemini 2.5 Pro 19.9/8.1, Gemini 3 Pro 50.5/10.8.
   - Claude Code: Claude 4 Sonnet 41.4/5.9, Kimi K2 40.3/8.6, Gemini 2.5 Pro 12.9/3.8, Gemini 3 Pro 34.9/6.5.
3. Security conditional on function (SecPass⊥FuncPass, measured on the subset of tasks all compared systems solve correctly, averaged across frameworks). By model: Claude 4 Sonnet 18.3%, Kimi K2 22.0%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 30.4%, Gemini 3 Pro 21.4%. By framework: SWE-Agent 23.3%, OpenHands 20.1%, Claude Code 17.4%. Gemini 3 Pro on SWE-Agent: FuncPass improves by more than 2x, security by 1.3x.
4. Mitigation (SWE-Agent + Claude 4 Sonnet only, Table 5). Generic baseline: 57.0 FuncPass / 11.8 SecPass. Self-selection (agent picks CWE types itself): 50.0 / 14.5. Oracle (true CWE given): 55.4 / 15.1. Self-selection costs -7.0 pp of functionality. Per the Figure 5 transition matrix, the share of tasks going from correct-and-secure to incorrect is 3.2%.
5. Task size (Table 9, SWE-Agent + Claude 4 Sonnet): FuncPass/SecPass is 66.9/15.4 on single-file tasks, 39.1/4.3 on 2 files, and 30.3/3.0 on more than 2 files.

QUOTES
- "Although 57% of the solutions from SWE-Agent with Claude 4 Sonnet are functionally correct, only 11.8% are secure." (Abstract, p.1)
- "Since one solution can always be secure if it does not implement any meaningful feature, we care only about the security of those functionally correct solutions." (Sec 4.1, p.6)

METHOD DETAILS WORTH KEEPING
- Task validity is checked by execution. The masked repo must fail both test sets. The vulnerable commit must pass functional and fail security tests. The fixed commit must pass both (p.5).
- Human audit by five experts of the security tests for 200 tasks (Appendix B.5): 6.5% were coupled to the ground-truth implementation, 93.5% checked the security property, 49.5% fully covered alternative secure implementations, and 44.0% might miss edge cases. After revision, 186 tasks remain.
- Qualitative case: a Django verify_password() reimplementation that returns early on an unusable password creates a timing side channel (username enumeration). It passes functional tests (Sec 4.3, Fig 8).

LIMITS
- Authors concede (Appendix E): Python only. Test outcomes are a proxy for security. CWE annotations and tests "may be insufficient". They do not claim coverage of all exploit modalities.
- Tasks are drawn from historically vulnerable features, so the benchmark is biased toward security-sensitive code. It does not give a base rate of insecure code in ordinary feature work.
- The task description deliberately omits security guidance.
- Mitigation was tested on one agent-model pair with two prompt strategies. It does not show that no mitigation works. The authors call the strategies "preliminary".
- Security is graded by tests written for the original fix, so false negatives and positives remain possible.
- Models are 2025 vintage (Claude 4 Sonnet, Kimi K2, Gemini 2.5 Pro and 3 Pro). The numbers will have dated.
- pass@1 only, a single run per task, with no variance reported.
- Compared systems differ in both model and framework. Subset-based SecPass⊥FuncPass depends on which tasks are in the intersection.

BUILDS ON
- SWE-bench (Jimenez et al., ICLR 2024) and the SWE-Agent, OpenHands (Wang et al., ICLR 2025) and Claude Code frameworks.
- Vulnerability-fix commit datasets ReposVul (Wang et al., 2024) and MoreFixes (Akhoundali et al., 2024).
- Security benchmarks BaxBench (Vero et al., 2025), CWEval (Peng et al., 2025), SecureAgentBench (Chen et al., 2025), ASE (Lian et al., 2025), SecCodePLT, SALLM and Asleep at the Keyboard (Pearce et al., 2025).
- "Vibe coding" is credited to Sarkar & Drosos (2025) and Fawzy et al. (2025).

BEST-FIT SECTION: Primary pick is notes/12-failure-modes.md "Measuring the wrong thing" (line 239). It is the "metric doesn't track what users care about" case, and the denominator logic matches the "Wrong denominator" bullet. A SecPass-style joint metric is the fix. Secondary pick is notes/06-evaluating-agents.md "Grade the outcome by state, not by words" (line 94), as a cross-link or one-line example. The "Pitfalls" list in 06 is a third option, as a new bullet: "Scoring function only, ignoring a second outcome dimension (security)". If only one place is allowed, use 12. In 06, the pitfall bullet is the tighter fit.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p.1), the task, agent and two test suites schematic, shows the dual grading. The better explainer of the claim is Table 3 (p.7), though it is a table, not a figure. Figure 5 (p.8), the generic-to-self-selection transition matrix, is the one that shows the trade-off.
